title: Coaching in Pairs or Threes.. and why this can be much better than coaching individuals er-than-coaching-individuals/
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington argues that coaching two or three teachers together, rather than one-to-one, may actually be preferable even without any time constraint, and lays out seven advantages of the paired or triad model. Group coaching surfaces a shared agenda -- teachers realise their challenges are common problems rather than individual weaknesses -- and pools a wider range of experience and ideas than a single coach-teacher pair could generate alone. It also depersonalises the process, reducing the observer/judge power dynamic that can creep into one-to-one coaching, and models the coaching dialogue itself to everyone present, which Sherrington argues sharpens the coach's own precision and discipline. He highlights that paired coaching creates public commitment to action steps and lets conversations continue organically between sessions, and that groups can run mini-rehearsals of scripts or feedback language in a way that feels too exposing in a strict one-to-one setting. Sherrington is equally direct about the drawbacks -- loss of personalisation, difficulty when teachers' goals diverge significantly, avoidance of direct individual challenges, and dependence on trust between the paired teachers -- and describes one school's solution of alternating between group and individual sessions to get the benefits of both.
points: Sherrington's central claim: even with unlimited time, he would still prefer coaching two or three teachers together over one-to-one, because of the pooled experience and depersonalisation it creates.
Group coaching turns action steps into public commitments shared with a colleague, which Sherrington argues secures follow-through better than a private commitment made only to the coach.

A concrete drawback he names is that paired coaching only works when teachers share similar challenges or goals -- if their practice diverges too far, the format collapses into two parallel conversations rather than one shared one.
One school's compromise -- alternating some sessions as group coaching and others as one-to-one -- lets Sherrington capture the benefits of both formats rather than choosing permanently between them.
quotes: I’m starting to think that, even if time was unlimited and not a constraint, with two or three people in a team to coach, I would prefer to coach them all together than one by one.
We don’t need to frame coaching as a critique of individual performance – it is about solving the common problems we all experience.
With two people there, you are much more explicitly focused on the technical aspects of the teaching challenge.

Another strong feature is that when teachers state their action steps for the next cycle, it’s not a private commitment to their coach; it’s a public statement of intent shared to at least one other colleague.

It's hard if teachers are at very different stages or have very different teaching goals. Paired coaching really relies on the teachers having similar challenges and goals so that you can talk about the same issues.
For sure, I’d like to argue that paired coaching with all its intrinsic benefits and time saving advantages should be elevated in the discourse.
